The current caseload reveals several patterns and anomalies warranting attention. First, **age data for accused individuals is highly incomplete**: of 92 distinct accused, only 17 have recorded ages (24–49 years, mean 31.5), while 75 have no age data [Document 1]. This limits analysis of demographic trends but highlights a potential gap in record-keeping.  

Second, **relationships between accused and complainants are predominantly with strangers**: 15 of 24 recorded relationships (across 10 FIRs) categorize the accused as “اجنبی” (stranger), suggesting a significant proportion of incidents involve no prior connection between parties [Document 2].  

Third, **seized property handling shows two distinct paths**: 13 items were sent to a forensic laboratory, and 7 are held for deceased heirs, indicating cases involving both criminal investigations (forensic analysis) and civil matters (inheritance) [Document 3].  

Fourth, **incident timing clusters in the evening**: 19 of 50 incidents with usable timestamps occurred between 18:00–23:59, making this the busiest time band (38% of timed cases), followed by the afternoon (32%) [Document 4]. Notably, 14 cases have timestamps of 00:00:00, which are excluded from time-of-day analysis due to lack of clock time [Document 4].  

Finally, **four accused individuals recur across multiple FIRs**: فیصل, طارق, شہزیب عرف شابی, and عاصم رشید each appear in **2 cases**, with FIR numbers fir-202-26, fir-401-26, fir-214-26, fir-891-24, fir-64-26, and fir-65-26 [Document 5]. This recurrence may signal ongoing involvement or networks requiring deeper investigation.  

These findings—particularly the incomplete age data, prevalence of stranger relationships, evening incident clustering, and recurring accused—stand out as non-routine aspects of the caseload.
